2.7 — Refactor Day: Moving Stats into the StatManager

In September you put coins and health on the Player, because that was the shortest way to a working game. It was the right call then. It is the wrong home now, and you are going to move them — without changing a single thing about how the game plays. That move has a name: refactor.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I move my stats off the player?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

Coins, health and the ceiling on health all live on the Player. That was the fastest way to make a game in September and it is the wrong home for them now: the cave mouths lead to scenes that build their own Player, and a number that lives on a Player is a number that belongs to one scene. Today nothing about the game changes except who owns the numbers — and that is called a refactor.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Notice which numbers are about the player and which are about the runSpeed, the body and the input belong to this Player in this room. Coins, current health and the cap belong to your run at this game. Same file today, two different lifetimes tomorrow — and only one of those lifetimes survives a scene change.Read: the coin branch you wrote in 2.1 and the damage method from 2.2.
  2. Build one object a scene load is not allowed to destroyA singleton: one static field holding the instance, an Awake() that claims it on the first load and calls DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject), and a second branch that destroys the copy every later load brings with it.Read: the Singleton row of the quick reference.
  3. Move the three fields across without renaming themcoins, health and maxHealth leave PlayerController and become fields on StatManager. A move, not a redesign — same names, same types, same starting values.Read: the fields you declared in 2.1 and capped in 2.3.
  4. Move the three methods, signed amounts and allChangeHealth(int amount), ChangeCoins(int amount) and Die() follow their fields. The signed-amount convention, the ceiling and the death rule travel together, because a rule and the value it protects are one thing.Read: the death rule you wrote in 2.2.
  5. Repoint every caller, and let the compiler find the ones you forgotDelete the fields from the player first, then read the errors. Every caller swaps a field on this for a method call on manager — the reference Start() looks up once.Read: the FindAnyObjectByType row of the quick reference.

Four of the five parts are housekeeping you have done before: declare a field, move a method, update a call site. One part has no precedent at all — the object the scene loader is not allowed to delete — and that is why this page walks it line by line.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Move my stats off the player" cannot be looked up — it is a decision about your own code. "Do not destroy this object when a new scene loads" can.

Your turn

Your three stat fields are public after this refactor, where everything you wrote in 2.1 was [SerializeField] private. Name one thing a public field lets another script do that a method would not — and one bug it makes possible.

The duplicate guard exists because Start (index 0) has its own StatManager and one cave mouth leads back to it. What would happen to your coins the moment you walked in, if that branch were deleted?

In the Editor ~15 min
  1. Project window → open Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs. It reads public class StatManager : MonoBehaviour { } — an empty stub that has been sitting in the project since Unit 2 doing nothing at all. Today it earns its place.
  2. Hierarchy → open Assets/_Scenes/Start.unity and find the StatManager object. Then open Overworld.unity and find the StatManager there as well. Two objects, same script. Write down what you think happens if you walk from one scene to the other.
  3. File → Build Profiles → Scene List (older tutorials call this Build Settings): Start (index 0) is first, which is the scene a built game loads by default — and it is one of the two that carries a manager.
  4. Game view → press Play in the Overworld and collect three coins. Watch the Console. Then stop, press Play again from Start (index 0), walk into the overworld and collect one coin. The number in the Console is the whole story, and it is the reason for today's work.
  5. Hierarchy → select the Player and read Inspector → Player Controller. Every number you are about to move — Coins, Health, Max Health — is a box you can watch change while you play. That is what you are giving up by moving them, and it is why the walkthrough keeps the prints.
In the Code ~20 min
APIWhat it gives youWhat it costs
public static StatManager original; A field that belongs to the class, not to an object — reachable with no reference and no search. It starts as null, and nothing claims it for you.
void Awake() Unity's earliest hook: it runs once per object, and every Awake() in a scene finishes before the first Start() runs. Order between two objects' Awake() methods is still not promised.
DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject) The object moves into a scene of its own that never unloads, so it survives every load from then on. It takes a whole GameObject, not a component.
FindAnyObjectByType<StatManager>() Hands back the first component of that type anywhere in the loaded scene. It searches, so it costs something — call it once, never in Update().
Debug.LogError(message) A Console line painted red, impossible to scroll past. It does not stop the game, so the broken behaviour still runs.
Architectural specification — this is a refactor, not a rewrite. Nothing your game does changes; what changes is where the numbers live. Answer these before you open the files.
  • The move. Which fields leave PlayerController, and which stay — and why does the one you keep belong to the player rather than to the run?
  • The owner. Which setup hook claims the slot, and what does its other branch do with a second copy?
  • The seam. Which single method may change health, and what ceiling does it enforce?
  • The callers. How will you find every place that used to reach for those fields — by reading the file, or by deleting them first?

Socratic: Who Owns a Number?

  1. Your stat fields are public after this refactor, where September taught you [SerializeField] private. What does public let another script do that a method call would not — and why might that be a problem in a project with more than one programmer?
  2. Start (index 0) already contains its own StatManager object. If you walk back to it later, what will be there — and what happens if nothing stops it from registering itself a second time?
  3. When you delete a field and let the compiler list your call sites, you are using a tool to find something you could have searched for by hand. Which is more reliable, and what does the answer tell you about why refactoring is usually a two-step job — delete, then compile?
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I keep my coins and my health when I change scenes?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs. This file has been public class StatManager : MonoBehaviour { } since Unit 2 — an empty stub that has never done anything. Today it becomes the owner. Every line is given; the only judgement is the order you read them in.

Step 1Claim a slot on load, and refuse to be destroyed

The mechanism the whole lesson exists for: one shared field, and a setup method that decides whether this copy is the original or a newcomer.

    public static StatManager original;

    void Awake()
    {
        if (original != null && original != this)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
            return;
        }

        original = this;
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }
  1. 1The one field every other script will reach for. public so they can, static so it belongs to the class rather than to any object, and typed StatManager because what it holds is this component. It starts as null — nothing has claimed it yet.Every word on that line is load-bearing. Drop static and the field becomes a fact about one object — and the object is exactly what a scene load destroys, so the slot would be empty again the moment you walked through a cave mouth. That is the whole trick: a static field is stored against the class, and the scene loader has no idea the class exists.
  2. 3The earliest hook Unity has. Every Awake() in a scene finishes before the first Start() runs, which is exactly the guarantee a singleton needs — somebody has to be first, and everything else must be able to assume they already were.Not Start(). Unity promises no order between two different scripts' Start() methods, so a script whose Start() happened to run before the manager's would read a null and throw — pointing at itself, not at the manager. Move this into Start() and the bug shows up only sometimes, which is the worst kind there is.
  3. 5Are you a newcomer? Two questions in one: is somebody already in the slot, and are they somebody other than you. The second half matters because Awake() runs on every load — including a reload where the slot already holds this very object.The && original != this half is the line people delete because it looks like caution. It is not. Without it, an object that runs Awake() twice destroys itself, and a singleton that destroys itself is a singleton that stops existing — with no error to explain it.
  4. 7The newcomer leaves, taking its fresh coins = 0 with it. gameObject is the whole object this component sits on — the StatManager object, not the script.
  5. 8Stop here, do not fall through. Without this line the newcomer is destroyed and still claims the slot on the way out, so original ends up pointing at an object that is about to stop existing. Every later caller then talks to a dead reference.
  6. 11this is the component this method is running inside — this very StatManager. Claim the slot with it, so every later caller reaches this object and the numbers on it.
  7. 12The one call in Unity that changes what a scene load is allowed to do. It moves the whole object into a scene of its own that never unloads, so it rides along through every load from now on.gameObject, not this. DontDestroyOnLoad is defined for whole objects, and it has to be: a component cannot outlive the GameObject carrying it. And notice what is not happening — nothing is being made permanent about the values. They are just sitting on an object the scene loader can no longer delete.
  8. 13One branch for the first scene and one for every scene after it. That pair is the singleton.

Step 2Move the three fields, and leave the names alone

They come off PlayerController and land here unchanged. Delete them from the player as you add them here — never both at once, or you will not know which file the compile error is about.

    public int health = 3;
    public int maxHealth = 3;
    public int coins;

    // ...and nothing else. PlayerController keeps its speed, its body
    // and its input. The numbers are not the player's business.
  1. 1Current health, with whatever starting value your player shipped with. Same name, same type, same number.public, where September taught you [SerializeField] private. Both work, and the difference is worth feeling rather than memorising: [SerializeField] puts the field in the Inspector and keeps other scripts out, while public puts it in the Inspector and lets any script in the project write it. Here the fields are public so the lesson stays about ownership; the methods below are what you should call, and they are where the rules live.
  2. 2The ceiling from 2.3.It travels in the same step as health, and that is the point. A ceiling is a fact about the value it bounds. Leave maxHealth behind on the player while health lives here and the rule gets enforced across two objects that are free to disagree.
  3. 3The coin count from 2.1. An int that starts at zero, which is what an int field does when you do not give it a value.
  4. 5That is the entire move. The player keeps what it is actually for — input, movement, the collision callbacks — and stops being the place the game keeps its numbers.The line between the two is the difference between a refactor and a mess: the player is how you move through the world, and the manager is what the world has done to you.

Step 3Move the three methods, and let them keep their names

The bodies come across from PlayerController with one word changed at most. If you find yourself improving a rule while you are in there, stop — you are rewriting, and now nothing you break is traceable to a single change.

    public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
    {
        health = health + amount;
        if (health > maxHealth)
        {
            health = maxHealth;
        }

        print("Health: " + health);
        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Die();
        }
    }

    public void ChangeCoins(int amount)
    {
        coins = coins + amount;
        if (coins < 0)
        {
            coins = 0;
        }

        print("Coins: " + coins);
    }

    public void Die()
    {
        health = maxHealth;
        coins = coins / 2;
        print("You died. Coins: " + coins);
    }
  1. 1Your 2.2 method, moved. Same name, same int amount, same meaning: a signed amount, where a negative number hurts and a positive one heals.Same name and same signature on purpose. Every call site in your project already reads ChangeHealth(-1) or ChangeHealth(1), so keeping the name means this refactor changes who is called and nothing else. Rename it and you are editing every caller by hand, hoping you found them all.
  2. 3The subtraction from 2.2, unchanged. -2 from the fireball takes two off; +1 from the potion puts one back.
  3. 4The cap from 2.3 — written as an if rather than a Mathf.Clamp(), which is what the build does. Either tool is correct; the point is that the ceiling is enforced here, on the only object that holds both numbers.This line is why the ceiling had to travel with the value. The rule now lives inside the only method that can change health, on the only object that holds it — so no caller, today or next month, can put health above the maximum.
  4. 6Snap to the ceiling rather than overflowing past it. A potion at full health does nothing, which is the behaviour you want and the reason the cap exists.
  5. 9Your Console readout, exactly as it was. Still worth keeping while you test: until 5.3 puts the numbers on screen, the Console is the only place you can see them.
  6. 10The other half of the 2.2 rule: what happens when health runs out.<= 0, not < 0. With a signed amount, health reaches exactly 0 on the hit that kills you, and a < 0 test would let you walk around at zero health for one more hit. Read your own 2.2 line before you copy this one — if yours says < 0, change it now and say why in your commit message.
  7. 12A call, not a print. The death rule is about to grow, and a named method is where a rule that grows belongs.
  8. 16Your 2.1 coin method, moved. Note the rename from ChangeCoin to ChangeCoins — singular to plural — so that it reads as the sibling of ChangeHealth: both take a signed amount, both are the only way in.
  9. 18The line from 2.1, with the 1 replaced by the parameter. A coin is ChangeCoins(1); a five-coin bonus needs no new code at all.
  10. 19The floor. Coins can be taken away — Die() takes half — and halves round down, so a player with one coin would otherwise be left at zero and a player at zero could go negative. A number on the screen that can read -1 is a bug the player can see.
  11. 21Clamp to the floor, the same shape as the ceiling above.
  12. 24Your 2.1 readout. Same deal as the health line — it is the instrument, not the feature.
  13. 27Public, because it moves. In 2.2 nothing outside the player called it. Now anything that resolves a death — a boss, a pit, a scene transition in Unit 5 — can call the same rule instead of reimplementing it.
  14. 29Refill. The build does not reload the scene and does not move the player: you keep playing from where you are, at full health, with half your money gone.2.2 offered you a choice here — reload the scene, reset the position, or just reset the numbers — and this is the option the build took. It is the cheapest one, and it is honest about being cheap: it exists so the game keeps running while you test everything else. A real death loop is Unit 8.
  15. 30The cost of dying. Integer division throws the remainder away, so 5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5 — and the floor in ChangeCoins is what keeps the result from ever going negative.
  16. 31The line that proves the rule ran. Three prints in one file, and each of them is a number you cannot otherwise see.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Three things have to match: the fields are gone from PlayerController rather than copied, the duplicate branch really is there — Start (index 0) holds a second StatManager and one cave mouth leads back to it — and your own rules came across from 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 exactly as you wrote them. The names are the ones every caller will use: original, ChangeHealth, ChangeCoins, Die.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// StatManager.cs - the numbers the player earned, on the one object a scene
// load is not allowed to destroy.
public class StatManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public int health = 3;
    public int maxHealth = 3;
    public int coins;

    public static StatManager original;

    void Awake()
    {
        // Somebody is already alive. This copy is the one that leaves - the
        // Start scene has its own manager, and you can walk back to it.
        if (original != null && original != this)
        {
            Destroy(gameObject);
            return;
        }

        original = this;
        DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);
    }

    public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
    {
        health = health + amount;

        // The ceiling from 2.3, on the only object that holds the value it
        // protects. No caller can get above it.
        if (health > maxHealth)
        {
            health = maxHealth;
        }

        print("Health: " + health);

        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Die();
        }
    }

    public void ChangeCoins(int amount)
    {
        coins = coins + amount;

        if (coins < 0)
        {
            coins = 0;
        }

        print("Coins: " + coins);
    }

    public void Die()
    {
        health = maxHealth;
        coins = coins / 2;
        print("You died. Coins: " + coins);
    }
}
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how does the player call the manager?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. The manager exists and nothing talks to it. This walkthrough is the other half of a refactor: delete first, compile, and let the errors tell you exactly which callers you missed. Five minutes of red underlines beats twenty minutes of guessing.

Step 1Delete the stat fields, then compile on purpose

Before you write a single new line. The file will not compile and that is the point — the compiler is the only complete list of call sites you will ever get.

    [SerializeField] private int coins;
    [SerializeField] private int health = 3;
    [SerializeField] private int maxHealth = 3;

// Ctrl/Cmd+S, then read the Console
  1. 1Delete. This line and the two below it are the ones that moved.
  2. 2Delete.
  3. 3Delete — along with ChangeCoin, ChangeHealth and Die from further down the file.
  4. 5Every place the player, the projectile or a pickup still touches one of those names is now an error, with a file and a line number. That list is the rest of this lesson.Work the errors top to bottom and recompile after each fix. Fixing five at once and compiling once turns a list of small, specific problems into one long, ambiguous one.

Step 2Look the manager up once, in Start()

The player needs a reference to the manager. It has found its own components with GetComponent() since 2.2 — this is the same idea for an object that is not on this GameObject.

    StatManager manager;

        manager = FindAnyObjectByType<StatManager>();

        if (manager == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("No StatManager in this scene.");
        }
  1. 1A field in the class body, beside rb and animator. Not serialized: you are not going to drag it in, the script is going to find it.
  2. 3One lookup, in Start(). It searches the loaded scene for the first component of that type and hands it back. GetComponent() only ever looks at this one GameObject; this asks the whole scene.Once, not every frame. The same rule as the body lookup in 2.2 and the scene name in 6.1: a thing that cannot change while the scene is loaded is looked up once and remembered. In Update() this search would run sixty times a second for an answer that never moves.
  3. 5The guard, and here it genuinely earns its place: two of the three scenes contain a Player, and only some of them contain a manager.
  4. 7Red, not a print. Debug.LogError paints the Console red and makes the failure impossible to scroll past — which is what you want for a scene that is missing a whole object, not for a number you are watching.A guard that hides a broken scene is worse than no guard. Logging and carrying on means the game runs, the coins do nothing, and the Console says why. Silently returning would look identical to working code until someone noticed their coin count never moved.

Step 3Repoint the callers — the part people forget

Each of these is one word changed: the receiver. The amount, the condition and the Destroy() beside it are all untouched.

            manager.ChangeCoins(1);
            manager.ChangeHealth(1);

            manager.ChangeHealth(-2);

        // Nothing else changes: movement, input, the tag checks and the
        // Destroy calls are all untouched. Only the receivers changed.
  1. 12.1's coin branch. coins = coins + 1; became a method call on the manager, and the Destroy(other.gameObject) underneath it stays exactly where it was.
  2. 22.3's potion. A positive amount heals, and the ceiling you just moved decides whether it does anything at all.
  3. 43.4's fireball. A negative amount hurts — the same signed-amount convention from 2.2, now arriving from a projectile instead of a spike. The Destroy(other.gameObject) that removes the bullet stays right below it.This is the line the whole refactor was for. The projectile used to hold a reference to the Player purely so it could call a damage method on it. It does not need one now: anything that can reach the manager can hurt you, and the rule that resolves the damage lives in exactly one file.
  4. 6That sentence is the definition of a refactor. If you find yourself rewriting a condition or "improving" a branch while you are in there, stop — you are rewriting.

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The test is negative and it is easy to run: search PlayerController.cs for the words coins, health and maxHealth, and the only hits left should be ChangeCoins and ChangeHealth — calls, not fields. // ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;

// PlayerController.cs - the stat fields and their three methods are gone.
// What is left is what the player is for: input, movement, and the callbacks
// that tell the manager something happened.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 4;
    bool isPlatformer = false;

    Rigidbody2D rb;
    StatManager manager;          // found once in Start(), never searched again

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
        manager = FindAnyObjectByType<StatManager>();

        if (manager == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("No StatManager in this scene. Start from the Start scene, or add one.");
        }

        // ... the scene-name gravity block from 6.1 ...
    }

    void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            manager.ChangeCoins(1);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }

        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Potion"))
        {
            manager.ChangeHealth(1);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }

        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("E_Fireball"))
        {
            manager.ChangeHealth(-2);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }
}
Build Lab: Prove the Move ~15 min

A refactor is only finished when you can show that nothing changed. Four checks, in this order:

CheckWhat it proves
Collect a coin The coin branch reaches the manager. Console says Coins: 1.
Walk into a spike The signed amount still hurts. Console says Health: 2.
Pick up a potion at full health The ceiling travelled with the value. Health stays at 3.
Take damage until death Die() runs from inside ChangeHealth. Health is back at max, coins are halved.
A refactor that also changes behaviour is not a refactor. If the jump feels different, the movement is slower, or a pickup stopped working while you were in these files, you touched something that was not part of the move. Put it back and commit the move on its own — a commit that says "moved stats to StatManager" should contain nothing else.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Say what a refactor is, and name the thing about your game that did not change
  • Explain why a static field survives a scene load when an instance field does not
  • Explain why the duplicate branch needs original != this, and why it needs return
  • Say why the ceiling and the death rule had to move with the values they protect
  • Find call sites by deleting a field and compiling, instead of searching by hand
  • Commit and push
